section_summary: The section closes a report on Japan’s 1947 elections, covering safeguards against interference by former neighborhood associations, voter turnout, invalid ballots, and the political implications of the results. It then contains diplomatic transmittals, articles debating Japan’s postwar future, a report on Japanese women’s political and social activities, correspondence about Toyohiko Kagawa, and a transmittal concerning letters to Occupation authorities.

subfiles.title: Report on the April 1947 Japanese elections, concluding pages
subfiles.about: Reviews electoral safeguards, participation, party results, and the Supreme Commander’s assessment of Japan’s 1947 elections.
subfiles.summary: The report describes action to exclude former neighborhood association leaders from election administration, efforts to reduce abstentions and invalid ballots, and paper shortages that constrained campaigning. It assesses the fairness of voting and counting, suggests improvements to future elections, and compares party support in 1946 and 1947. It finds strong conservative control locally despite Social Democratic gains nationally. The final page reproduces MacArthur’s April 27 statement welcoming the elections and the new constitution.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2114 transmitting “Satellite Japan”
subfiles.from: Everett F. Drumright, American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Transmits Sir Paul Butler’s Spectator article on Japan’s prospective alignment with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Drumright recommends Butler’s article to officers concerned with Japan and other Far Eastern issues.

subfiles.title: “Satellite Japan”
subfiles.about: Argues that Japan may become an American-aligned satellite amid worsening United States–Soviet relations.
subfiles.summary: Butler considers American predominance in Japan preferable to Soviet influence, while examining British Commonwealth interests in a peace settlement. He anticipates Japanese economic reconstruction and export growth under American support, but warns against renewed illusions about Japan’s political intentions.

subfiles.title: Copy of “Satellite Japan”
subfiles.about: Repeats the enclosed Spectator article on Japan’s likely position in an American sphere of influence.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Butler’s argument for American predominance, Japanese economic recovery, and continued caution about Japan’s future political conduct.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement form for Despatch No. 1306
subfiles.about: Identifies an attached copy as the record copy replacing an unreturned original despatch.
subfiles.summary: Records replacement of the missing action copy of Tokyo Despatch No. 1306.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1306 transmitting non-military activity summations
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards SCAP summations of non-military activities in Japan for May and June 1947.
subfiles.summary: Sends four copies of each monthly summation and explains the delayed May report.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1320 transmitting “Japanese Women”
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a SCAP report on Japanese women’s political, economic, and social activities.
subfiles.summary: Sends five copies of the Civil Information and Education Section’s report “Japanese Women.”

subfiles.title: “Japanese Women,” Publications Analysis No. 95
subfiles.from: Civil Information and Education Section, Media Analysis Division, SCAP
subfiles.about: Surveys Japanese magazine discussions of women’s political participation, birth control, and labor rights.
subfiles.summary: The report reviews praise and criticism of women Diet members and calls for women’s political education. It summarizes competing views on birth control, population, family reform, employment, strikes, and women’s participation in unions. A final source list names the magazines and writers surveyed.

subfiles.title: Record-copy replacement form for Despatch No. 1328
subfiles.about: Identifies an attached copy as the record copy replacing an unreturned original despatch.
subfiles.summary: Records replacement of the missing action copy of Tokyo Despatch No. 1328.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1328 on the scope of Japanese cabinet orders
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits SCAP instructions limiting the use of Japanese cabinet orders for substantive legislation.
subfiles.summary: Explains that substantive measures should pass through the National Diet under Article 41 of the constitution.

subfiles.title: Routing note requesting a reply to the Johnson letter
subfiles.about: Requests suggestions for answering an attached letter or a copy of any direct reply.
subfiles.summary: Asks for reply suggestions concerning the attached correspondence.

subfiles.title: Kenneth E. Johnson’s inquiry about Toyohiko Kagawa
subfiles.to: Department of State, Department of Public Information
subfiles.about: Asks whether reports that Japanese Christian leader Toyohiko Kagawa is being held for trial are true.
subfiles.summary: Johnson seeks official information about Kagawa’s status and lists other offices he has contacted.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Kenneth E. Johnson
subfiles.from: Frank E. Schuler Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Johnson’s question about Kagawa’s reported detention and purge status.
subfiles.summary: The Department has no evidence of detention; Kagawa’s purge screening remains undecided.

subfiles.title: William R. Mathews’s letter to Robert T. Oliver
subfiles.about: Disputes Oliver’s criticism of United States policy toward Japan and Korea.
subfiles.summary: Mathews argues for Japanese economic self-support through trade and urges Oliver to avoid disparaging officials’ decisions concerning Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to William R. Mathews
subfiles.from: J. K. Penfield, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of a copy of Mathews’s letter to Robert T. Oliver.
subfiles.summary: Thanks Mathews for sharing his views on Far Eastern problems.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2398 transmitting “Democracy in Japan”
subfiles.from: Everett F. Drumright, American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Transmits an Economist article assessing Japan’s postwar democracy and social reforms.
subfiles.summary: Highlights the article’s concern that economic collapse and incomplete reforms threaten democracy if Occupation forces withdraw.

subfiles.title: “Democracy in Japan”
subfiles.about: Assesses whether Japan’s externally introduced constitutional and social reforms can sustain democracy.
subfiles.summary: The article contrasts favorable and skeptical assessments of the new regime. It argues that land reform, dissolution of the zaibatsu, trade recovery, and adequate imports matter more to democratic stability than constitutional design alone. It concludes that economic collapse and incomplete reform leave democracy vulnerable to an immediate end of the American Occupation.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1354 transmitting a report on Japanese letters to Occupation authorities
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a September 23, 1947 survey of views expressed in Japanese letters to Occupation authorities.
subfiles.summary: Forwards five copies of SCAP Analysis and Research Division Report No. 15.
